title: Tariff Refund Rescue for Micro-Importers
one_liner: A flat-fee triage, protest and pooled-filing service that recovers IEEPA tariff refunds for small importers whose entries fell outside the automated CBP refund system.
customer: US importers of record with roughly $5K-$250K of IEEPA duties paid: direct-import Shopify/Amazon/Etsy sellers, small distributors, restaurants and retailers who imported containers. Not the big players, who already have trade lawyers. They pay a flat audit fee plus a success fee on money recovered. Lenders and claim buyers are a secondary customer.
problem: The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs on Feb 20, 2026. CBP's CAPE refund portal opened Apr 20 and initially covered only about 63% of entries. Entries that were finally liquidated, are under protest, or have mixed statuses fall outside it. The 180-day protest clock runs per entry. Trade lawyers quote $10,000-$15,000, which wipes out a $15,000 refund. Small importers hold these stuck entries and cannot justify the fees, while interest accrues at 6%.
solution: Software plus a small ops desk. The importer uploads ACE reports or grants read-only ACE access. The tool sorts every entry into CAPE-eligible, protest window still open (with a per-entry deadline calendar), or finally liquidated. It auto-builds CAPE declarations for self-filers, protest packets, and a standardized pooled Court of International Trade joinder or complaint filed by a partner trade law firm at a flat per-importer price. It also verifies and bundles small claims into $20M+ pools that lenders and claim buyers will finance. That gives importers cash now instead of a 60-90+ day wait. Non-lawyers cannot share legal fees, so the legal work is a separate flat fee to partner counsel.
why_now: CAPE Phase 1 opened Apr 20, 2026 and Phase 2 on Jun 29. The CIT issued reliquidation orders for finally liquidated entries on Jul 15 and Jul 21, but it is unclear whether non-litigants must sue. In late September 2026, coverage says refunds remain 'caught between Customs and the courts'. Protest windows on spring-2026 liquidations are expiring right now. The Feb-Sept 2026 window will not repeat.
revenue_model: $99-$299 triage fee, credited toward a 7-12% success fee on refunds recovered (software and ops, not legal fees). A flat pass-through fee to partner counsel for CIT filings. Portfolio-packaging fee, paid by the lender or claim buyer, on pooled small claims that meet institutional minimums.
non_obvious_insight: The money is in the long tail, not the big importers. The US Chamber says 300,000+ companies and about $166B in duties are affected, across 53M+ entries (https://www.uschamber.com/economy/tariff-refunds-faq-what-small-businesses-need-to-know-after-supreme-courts-ruling). A Sept 2026 report says small importers are stuck because $10K-$15K legal costs can exceed the refund itself, and that importers have entries spread across unliquidated, protest-window and final statuses at the same time (https://kvia.com/stacker-international/2026/09/22/months-after-ieepa-tariffs-were-struck-down-some-refunds-remain-caught-between-customs-and-the-courts/). Meanwhile the refund-claims secondary market is estimated at up to $100B, trading at up to 60 cents on the dollar, but lenders want a minimum $10M loan against at least $20M of claims (https://www.sidley.com/en/insights/newsupdates/2026/04/ieepa-tariff-refund-claims-key-considerations-for-lenders-borrowers-and-claims-purchasers). Nobody aggregates the small claims. The wedge is a per-entry deadline calendar and standardized filing packet, plus pooling for liquidity, not legal advice.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: build an ACE-report parser that outputs entry buckets and protest deadlines, and sign a flat-fee arrangement with a licensed customs broker and a CIT-admitted trade attorney. Days 8-20: post the free 'which of my entries are stuck?' triage tool in small-importer communities (Shopify and Amazon private-label groups, freight forwarder mailing lists, Reddit r/importing). Target 30 uploads. Days 21-30: convert 8-10 importers to paid protest or pooled filings, and record the recovered dollars as case studies for the lender pooling pitch.

title: Exposure Response Desk for Vibe-Coded Apps
one_liner: A fix-and-legal-decision service for founders whose AI-built apps leaked user data, delivering an RLS lockdown, an access-log check and a breach-notification memo.
customer: Non-technical founders and small businesses that shipped apps on Lovable, Bolt, Replit or Cursor with a Supabase backend, and small agencies that build such apps for local clients. They pay $149-$499 per incident plus $29/month monitoring.
problem: On Sept 25, 2026 UpGuard reported about 16,000 Supabase databases publicly exposing names, home addresses, phone numbers, passwords, auth tokens, private conversations and license plate records. AI coding tools write SQL migrations where Row-Level Security defaults to off, and founders never turn it on. An earlier flaw, CVE-2025-48757, exposed 170+ Lovable apps. Owners do not know how to fix it without breaking the app, whether anyone actually accessed the data, or whether they now have a legal duty to notify users and regulators.
solution: Not another scanner, since ShipSafe and VibeAppScanner already exist. This is a response desk. (1) The owner authorizes a read-only check on their own project. (2) The tool generates and tests an RLS policy pull request for common patterns (owner-only rows, public read and owner write, storage buckets) that does not break the app. (3) It reviews available Supabase API and Postgres logs to estimate whether anonymous-key access from unknown sources occurred. (4) A partner privacy attorney's state-by-state and GDPR decision tree produces a notification-or-not memo. (5) It drafts user notices and an evidence packet for the owner's cyber insurer. Continuous monitoring is upsell.
why_now: The UpGuard disclosure is three days old, and Cursor AI is the fastest-growing Glimpse trend of 2026 (+2,213%), with Cyber Insurance up 763% on Exploding Topics. Mass disclosures of this kind will keep recurring as more founders ship AI-built apps. Legal clocks (GDPR 72 hours, state laws with 30-60 day windows) create urgency at exactly the moment the owner learns of the exposure.
revenue_model: $149 lockdown-only tier, $499 lockdown plus log review plus notification memo and letters, $29/month continuous monitoring, and $99/client wholesale packages for agencies. Later: referral fees from cyber insurers and privacy counsel.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone sells detection. Nobody sells the 'now what', and the mission-critical question for an owner is legal, not technical. The trigger is public and fresh: UpGuard found ~16,000 exposed Supabase databases, the root cause is that AI-written migrations leave RLS off, and Supabase's CISO says security 'ultimately remains a shared responsibility' (https://startupfortune.com/upguard-found-16000-supabase-databases-leaking-user-data-to-the-open-web/). CVE-2025-48757 previously exposed 170+ Lovable apps, and the common failure is founders who cannot debug RLS (https://www.superblocks.com/blog/lovable-vulnerabilities). The scanner market already exists (https://vibeappscanner.com/lovable-security), which means paid demand is proven while the response step remains unowned. Cursor AI's +2,213% growth is the #1 item at https://meetglimpse.com/trends/.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: build the read-only exposure checker that owners run on their own project, plus an RLS policy generator for the five most common patterns. Days 8-15: co-author a 'Supabase RLS was off, what now? (24-hour plan)' guide with a privacy attorney and publish it for SEO and Reddit (r/lovable, r/supabase, Indie Hackers). Days 16-30: sell 20 lockdown fixes at $149-$199 and sign 2 small agencies at wholesale rates. Skip scanning anyone's databases without their authorization.

title: Allergen Drift Alerts for School Cafeterias
one_liner: A weekly diff engine over the open Open Food Facts and USDA Branded Food Products data that tells school nutrition directors when a product on their order guide silently changed its allergens.
customer: K-12 school district food service directors and their purchasing co-ops and state agencies (about 13,000 US districts). A parent-facing paid alert tier for families of children with severe allergies is a secondary market.
problem: Distributors substitute products and manufacturers reformulate without notice. After sesame became the ninth major US allergen, some bakeries began adding sesame on purpose. Directors keep allergen lists in spreadsheets built from last year's spec sheets. Recalls are announced only after exposure, and cooks get blamed for what is really supplier drift.
solution: Ingest the district's order guide (Sysco, US Foods, Gordon Food Service item lists) and match SKUs to GTINs. Track ingredient statements and allergen declarations over time using Open Food Facts revision history and the monthly USDA Branded Food Products (GDSN) releases. Send a weekly 'allergen drift' report and immediate alerts when an allergen is added, a 'may contain' changes, or a substitution appears. Auto-update the district's allergen matrix and menu labels.
why_now: Branded-food data goes stale quickly and USDA now publishes monthly GDSN updates. Reformulation churn following the 2023 sesame rule and supply-chain substitutions is high. Open Food Facts has reached scale, and diffing it is cheap while no one sells the diff.
revenue_model: USD 500-1,500 per district per year, tiered by SKU count. State-agency or co-op bulk licenses. Parent alert tier at USD 3-5 per month.
non_obvious_insight: Most cafeteria allergen incidents trace to a silent supplier change, not to cooking error, so the value is monitoring the upstream data exhaust that already exists and is free. Directors will pay for peace of mind and liability evidence, not for a new database.
first_30_days: Build the diff pipeline for the 300 most common K-12 SKUs. Publish a free weekly 'Allergen Drift Report' newsletter aimed at food service directors and state school nutrition associations to build trust. Offer 5 districts a free SKU-matching of their full order guide. Convert to paid alerts with the first two districts that catch a real change.

title: Tariff Refund Recovery for Dead Importers
one_liner: A contingency service that finds failed or dormant importers whose IEEPA refund claims are stranded, revives them or works through their bankruptcy trustee, and files the claims through a licensed broker.
customer: Chapter 7 trustees and ABC assignees of failed importers, plus founders of dissolved or dormant small importers. They pay 20-30% of recovered dollars. Secondary customers are claim buyers who want vetted entry-level claim files.
problem: The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs on Feb 20, 2026. CBP is now refunding through CAPE in phases: Phase 1 opened Apr 20 for unliquidated and recently liquidated entries, Phase 2 came in June, and Phase 3 (late July) covers finally liquidated entries only for importers who sued at the CIT. Refunds go to the importer of record (or the broker who filed the entry). Every entry has its own clock, including the 180-day protest window. A large tail of small importers closed or went dark during the 2025 tariff shock. Their refunds are six-figure receivables spread across hundreds of ACE entries. They appear on nobody's balance sheet, and nobody at the dead company is watching for them. A trustee liquidating the estate usually does not know the asset exists.
solution: Build an entry-level refund estimator from public bill-of-lading data, HTS lines, country of origin and the IEEPA rate schedule. Cross-match importer names against state dissolution lists and PACER filings to rank stranded claims by likely dollar value. Then run the recovery: (1) approach trustees with an asset-discovery letter and a court-approvable contingency engagement; (2) for dissolved entities, reinstate the corporation under state law, re-enroll ACH, and file CF-4811 designations where needed; (3) have a licensed broker file CAPE declarations for the entries that broker filed; (4) send finally liquidated entries to partner trade counsel for CIT reliquidation orders under the July 17 order. The moat is a licensed-broker partner plus a pipeline of claims that nobody else is hunting.
why_now: IEEPA was struck down Feb 20, 2026. CAPE phases rolled out Apr-Jul 2026, and the July 17 CIT order created a court-driven Phase 3. Per-entry deadlines are now running. Existing refund tools (deadline trackers and CAPE filing helpers) all sell to living importers who are already paying attention. Nobody productized the orphaned-claim hunt.
revenue_model: 20-30% contingency on refunds recovered, plus interest. Trustee engagements are approved by the bankruptcy court as contingency fee arrangements. A secondary line sells diligenced claim packages to claim buyers at a flat fee per package.
non_obvious_insight: The refund is attached to the importer-of-record number, not to whoever was actually hurt, and only the IOR or the filing broker can claim it in the early phases. Brokers hold the entry data but their powers of attorney die with the client, and chasing a dead client is unbillable work, so nobody does it. A broker can still file CAPE for entries it filed, which makes the broker the key that unlocks these claims. Outsiders see the refund as a tax-accounting topic. Insiders see it as an unclaimed-property hunt across ACE.
first_30_days: Week 1: pull 2025 importer-level volumes for China, Vietnam, India and other tariffed origins from ImportYeti or a cheap paid BOL feed, then estimate each importer's IEEPA duty. Week 2: cross-match against CA, NY, TX, FL and NJ dissolution records and PACER chapter 7 and ABC filings, and rank the top 150 targets above about $50k. Week 3: send trustees a one-page asset-discovery letter, since trustee contact info is public, and have a trade lawyer draft the contingency engagement. Week 4: sign the first 3-5 estates, or dormant founders, and file the first CAPE declarations through the partner broker.

title: Signed Eyewitness Network for Ports and Sanctions
one_liner: A network of ship, plane and port spotters and local creators paid per provenance-signed capture (verified time, place and device), sold first to maritime insurers and sanctions teams and next to Coast Guard, Navy and intelligence analysts.
customer: Sanctions-compliance teams at banks, commodity traders and marine insurers or P&I brokers ($40-150 per verified task, $2-5K/month watchlist subscriptions). Later buyers are Coast Guard, CBP, NGA and defense OSINT analysts through SBIR or commercial solutions openings.
problem: Open-source analysis is bottlenecked on 'who shot this and when', not on analysis. AI fakes and unverified feeds enter analytic workflows: a SOCOM analyst's chatbot fabricated a cargo manifest and aircraft were airborne before the error was caught, while Maven now has 100K+ users and leaders admit gaps in logistics data visibility. Hobbyist spotters and drone and dashcam creators already sit at chokepoints, but their images cannot be trusted, priced or bought.
solution: Buyers post look-and-verify tasks ('is tanker X at berth Y today?'). Spotters reply with C2PA-signed captures from phones with native content credentials (prior knowledge: recent Pixel and Samsung models). The platform validates the signature chain, GNSS and time, and cross-checks sun angle, weather and AIS, then packages an analyst-ready evidence artifact with a spotter reputation score. Buyers purchase a signed artifact, not labor, so this is not a freelancer marketplace.
why_now: Native camera signing shipped on mainstream phones (prior knowledge) and C2PA reached spec 2.3, so no proprietary hardware is needed. Sanctions and shadow-fleet enforcement and the 2026 Iran conflict raise verification demand, and GenAI.mil put AI summarization in front of 2M users, making trusted ground-truth inputs the scarce resource.
revenue_model: Per-task fees with a 30% platform take, watchlist subscriptions, and government contracts later.
non_obvious_insight: AI is making analysis abundant and cheap while trusted ground truth stays scarce. The hobbyist spotter community is an existing, unpaid, reputation-rich sensor network, and because phones now sign captures a two-person team can build the verification layer instead of hardware.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 spotters from ship- and plane-spotting forums in two port cities. Take 10 paid pilot tasks at about $75 from a marine insurance broker or sanctions consultancy, build the verification pipeline around C2PA validation plus AIS cross-checks, and then apply to an SBIR or commercial solutions opening on commercial ground truth.

title: Verified-MW Truth Feed for Data Center Load
one_liner: A probability score and satellite-plus-permit verification of every large-load request, so planners and investors can tell the real 42 GW from the 201 GW of paper.
customer: Utility load-forecast and IRP teams, ISOs, state PUC staff and consumer advocates. Hedge funds, infrastructure investors and equipment makers buy the same feed as alternative data.
problem: About 36.6 GW is under construction versus about 201 GW 'in planning'. Developers file duplicate requests at several utilities, utilities over-forecast, and ratepayers fund the generation and wires built for load that never shows up. Even xAI's Memphis battery is '2.8 GWh counted versus 3.3 GWh claimed' and nobody verifies it.
solution: Fuse interconnection filings, zoning and permit records, tax abatements, transformer and switchgear procurement signals, construction imagery (SAR and optical), thermal signatures of cooling plants and tariff deposits into a per-project probability of energization by date and MW online. Ship it as an API, quarterly reports and exhibits usable in regulatory proceedings.
why_now: Large-load requests are exploding, utilities are adding deposit rules, and cheap satellite data plus LLM document parsing lets a three-person team do this.
revenue_model: $30-500k a year per investor subscription and $75-300k per utility or ISO, with discounted licenses for consumer advocates.
non_obvious_insight: The most expensive number in the grid is the load forecast, and it is built from self-reported requests. Hedge funds already want the same data for AI-capex tracking, so they can fund a public-interest product.
first_30_days: Build datasets for Virginia, Ohio and Texas. Publish a 'phantom load index'. Sell three alternative-data subscriptions at $30-50k. Offer free trials to two consumer advocate offices.

title: Executive Physicals for Union Trades Members
one_liner: Mobile 'Physical Days' at union halls and apprenticeship centers that give tradespeople the CEO-style cardiometabolic checkup, sold to the multiemployer health funds that pay their claims.
customer: Trustees and administrators of Taft-Hartley multiemployer health and welfare funds (building trades, Teamsters, food and commercial workers) and self-insured municipal and transit plans. First buyer: the fund of a 2,000-member electricians' or pipefitters' local.
problem: Workers 45-64 in the trades carry high rates of hypertension, sleep apnea, hearing loss, silica or dust lung exposure and undetected heart disease, yet they work 6am shifts and cannot make weekday clinic hours. Funds face rising costs (employers say GLP-1 drug costs loom large in the 2026 Business Group on Health survey) but their prevention is a voucher for an annual physical with low uptake. Corporate wellness vendors are built for white-collar campuses, not job sites.
solution: A 45-minute station circuit at the union hall or training center: validated blood pressure, fingerstick lipids and A1c (ApoB by send-out), single-lead ECG for atrial fibrillation, spirometry for dusty trades, audiogram, a STOP-BANG screen with a hand-off home sleep test, grip and gait, and FIT kits. A physician or NP reviews results the same day. Intermediate-risk members get a pre-booked $75-150 coronary calcium scan at a partner imaging center, and members with findings get a fast lane through a care navigator. Occupation-specific add-ons: sleep apnea for drivers, hearing and silica for construction. Fixed-fee pricing with no referral kickbacks.
why_now: GLP-1 spending has made plan sponsors receptive to prevention offsets. Point-of-care devices are now small and cheap enough to run a full circuit from two suitcases. Skilled-trades labor is aging and scarce, so trustees have a genuine interest in keeping members working and healthy longer.
revenue_model: $150-250 per participant paid by the fund, quarterly repeat days, plus optional shared-savings on downstream claims after the first year; add-on family-member days for spouses.
non_obvious_insight: Unions and multiemployer funds are the last pooled buyer with a 30-year time horizon on each member, so they are among the few payers who can actually capture the return on prevention (a corporate employer loses the employee after three years). Trustees are elected by the workers, so 'the same physical executives pay $5,000 for' is politically powerful. Elite prevention has to be sold where the payer keeps the member long enough to profit.
first_30_days: Get an introduction through an apprenticeship training center director or a local business manager. Offer a free or at-cost Physical Day for 40 members, staffed by a physician partner and two techs (roughly $6k in costs). Collect anonymized data on undiagnosed hypertension, high ApoB, apnea risk and hearing loss. Bring a one-page summary to the trustees at their next quarterly meeting comparing the cost of 30 physicals to one avoided cardiac event. Aim to sign a recurring contract within 4-5 months.

title: Cancellation Compliance for Regional Gym Chains
one_liner: A drop-in cancel-and-freeze portal that meets each state's auto-renewal rules and writes straight into the billing system.
customer: Regional gym and studio chains with 10-300 locations still using in-person or certified-mail cancellations, and franchisors.
problem: The FTC's national click-to-cancel rule was vacated in July 2025, but enforcement continues (the FTC sued Fitness International/LA Fitness over cancellation hurdles), state auto-renewal laws demand online cancellation if you joined online, and New York City's own click-to-cancel rule takes effect October 1, 2026. Chains run legacy contracts and billing where cancellation is manual, so exposure is AG settlements and class actions.
solution: A white-labeled 'Cancel, Pause, Downgrade' portal with a jurisdiction rules engine (notice periods, save-offer limits, refund proration, confirmations) that writes to the chain's billing platform through API or RPA, with audit logs and legally bounded retention offers.
why_now: NYC's October 1, 2026 deadline, the FTC's restart of subscription rulemaking, and active state AG scrutiny create a dated trigger with budget.
revenue_model: $150-400 per location per month plus $2k setup; share of saved revenue on approved retention flows.
non_obvious_insight: Compliance opens the door, retention pays for it: a compliant flow with legally allowed save offers often lifts net retention versus the friction chains use today, so the CFO buys it. The moat is the multi-state rules matrix plus billing-system integrations.
first_30_days: Build a rules matrix for 10 states plus NYC with a consumer-protection lawyer, sell a $1k mystery-shop 'compliance scan' of each chain's cancellation flow to 20 regional chains, and convert two into design partners.

title: Pay-on-Close Homebuyer Readiness for Builders
one_liner: A builder-funded coaching and underwriting-repair program for the roughly half of showroom visitors who cannot yet qualify, paid per closing instead of through rate buydowns.
customer: Production and regional builders and their affiliated mortgage companies. The builder pays $2,000-$5,000 per attributable closing.
problem: Lennar says nearly 50% of visitors in many markets cannot immediately qualify for a mortgage, and it gives about 12% of price in incentives on a $372K average price, or roughly $45K per home. KB Home's cancellation rate is 18% of gross orders (up from 17%), and it makes 'minor adjustments' to keep buyers qualified. Builders spend heavily on lowering the monthly payment and almost nothing on fixing the reasons buyers fail underwriting.
solution: A 60-120 day cohort program runs alongside the builder's sales funnel for prospects who fail pre-qualification. It has four parts: (1) debt-to-income triage with a plan to pay down or restructure the few accounts that cause most failures, (2) lender-coordinated rapid rescoring, (3) co-borrower matching and down-payment-assistance navigation across state housing finance agencies, employer housing programs and gift rules, and (4) rent and utility payment reporting. Milestones are shared with the builder's lender through a dashboard. The vendor is paid only when a buyer the program touched closes on a home in the builder's community.
why_now: Mortgage rates are rising again (Paychex references a recent 25 bp Fed increase), and Lennar says rate-buydown costs are climbing. Resale inventory is at a decade high and is competing directly with new homes. KB Home's Executive Chairman says pricing is declining in more markets. The cheapest lever left is converting buyers who are near qualification.
revenue_model: $2,000-$5,000 success fee per closed home attributable to a program participant. Optional $300 per enrolled prospect for the coaching workload, credited against the success fee. Lender referral fees where permitted and disclosed.
non_obvious_insight: Incentive budgets buy payment relief, not qualification, and the qualification gap is large. Lennar's Stuart Miller says nearly 50% of visitors cannot immediately qualify, average incentives are about 12% of a $372K price, and buydown costs are rising with rates (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/17/lennar-len-q3-2026-earnings-call-transcript/). KB Home reports an 18% cancellation rate, an 85% mortgage capture rate and 'minor adjustments' to keep buyers qualified, and buyers 'want to play the market and hope that rates come down' (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/23/kb-home-kbh-q3-2026-earnings-call-transcript/). Credit-repair vendors have a poor reputation, and lenders have no incentive to coach a borrower for months. A builder paying per closing, the way it pays a broker, is a distribution model none of them have.
first_30_days: Approach 10 regional builders (100-1,000 homes a year) and their affiliated lenders, offering a free 60-day pilot in 1-2 communities. Pull the builder's list of leads that failed pre-qualification in the last 6 months, ask a partner loan officer to tag the failure reason, and run a manual outreach and coaching pass with two HUD-certified housing counselors. Track conversions weekly and sign a success-fee agreement once 3 closings are attributable.

title: Year-Round Books for Immigrant-Community Tax Storefronts
one_liner: Give community tax preparers WhatsApp-native, in-language AI bookkeeping so they can serve their small-business clients all year.
customer: Independent tax storefronts in Latino, Vietnamese, Korean, Chinese and other immigrant communities, each serving 100-500 micro-business clients (taquerias, nail salons, owner-operator truckers, cleaners, roofing crews) who show up with a shoebox once a year.
problem: The clients have no monthly books. Preparers can't do year-round bookkeeping without adding headcount, and they cannot afford Intuit's or H&R Block's offering. Silicon Valley assumes better AI will close the trust gap, but these owners trust a person who speaks their language.
solution: White-label intake through WhatsApp, WeChat or KakaoTalk: the client sends receipt photos and voice notes in their language, and AI drafts the ledger and a monthly P&L. The preparer reviews exceptions in a queue and sends a plain-language summary. Sales tax, payroll deposits and quarterly estimated tax reminders are included. All output carries the preparer's brand.
why_now: Multilingual and code-switched voice transcription became reliable in 2025-26. IRS Direct File ended for 2026, and Intuit cut 17% of staff while opening about 600 offices and 20 TurboTax storefronts, which suggests trust stays human and local.
revenue_model: $99/month per storefront plus $12 per client per month, or a 30% revenue share on a $150 per client monthly bookkeeping fee.
non_obvious_insight: The trust problem is already solved by a human who is embedded in the community. What the preparer lacks is leverage, and the incumbents are hiring storefronts, not selling to them. AI turns a seasonal tax business into a year-round one.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 storefronts in one metro through ITIN and tax-prep associations and Spanish-language radio. Pilot with five clients each on WhatsApp Business. Charge nothing until the storefronts see retention and added revenue, then set the per-client price.

title: Orphan Lien Clearance Desk for Title Agents
one_liner: A flat-fee curative service that proves dead solar fixture filings and other zombie liens are dead (or gets them released) so home closings stop stalling.
customer: Independent title and escrow agencies and real estate attorneys in high-solar states (AZ, CA, FL, TX, NJ, NC, NV, CO), billed per file and usually paid by the seller at closing. Listing agents in solar-heavy markets are a second channel.
problem: Sunnova filed Chapter 11 in June 2025 (500,000+ customers), Mosaic and PosiGen followed, and the residential solar credit ended for 2026 installs, so thousands of homes carry UCC-1 fixture filings and recorded solar-lease notices held by dead, merged or reassigned entities. Title examiners flag every one. Agents can't tell who holds the debt now, whether the filing is even still legally effective, or how to get a termination, so closings slip days or weeks. The people currently serving this are consumer SEO and lead-gen sites, not the title agents who actually need it solved on a deadline.
solution: Per-file lien autopsy delivered in 48 hours. (1) Pull the recorded instrument and any continuation or termination filings from the county index and the Secretary of State. (2) Compute lapse under UCC 9-515 (five years unless continued in the six-month window). (3) Trace the assignment and servicer chain through bankruptcy dockets and servicer notices. (4) Deliver either an underwriter-ready 'lapsed, no exception' memo, or a payoff/estoppel request plus a pre-drafted termination (UCC-3, or debtor-filed termination where the statute allows) recorded in that county's required format. Recorded memoranda of lease, which do not lapse, get a release workflow instead. Later expand the same engine to satisfied-but-never-released mortgages, expired judgment liens, dead PACE liens and resurfaced zombie second mortgages.
why_now: 2025-2026 solar installer bankruptcies (Sunnova, Mosaic, PosiGen) and the end of the residential solar credit produced the largest single wave of orphaned fixture filings ever recorded. 2018-2021 installs are now hitting their five-year lapse dates just as those homes come to market. Title agents are short-staffed and want to outsource curative work, and an LLM can read county index entries and bankruptcy docket text cheaply.
revenue_model: Flat fee of about $395-$900 per cleared file, contingent on clear-to-close. Agencies with volume pay $299/month plus a reduced per-file rate. White-label API for underwriters and closing software later.
non_obvious_insight: Half the 'problem liens' in solar-heavy counties are already legally dead, but the county index never shows lapse, so examiners treat a 2019 fixture filing as live forever. Clerks watch continuation filings come in, and most small installers never filed one. The work is proof of death, not payoff. Insiders also know the recorded 'notice of lease' is a different animal that never lapses, and that a clerk must record a debtor-filed termination on its face, since the office is ministerial.
first_30_days: Offer the first five files free to 3-5 independent title agencies in Phoenix, Tampa and Sacramento. Build the lapse calculator and county-index lookups for about 10 counties. Get one regional agent underwriter to accept a standard lapse-memo format. Then price at $495 per file and ask each agency for a testimonial and two referrals to listing agents.

title: Safe-Deposit Box Successor With Heir Protocol
one_liner: A bonded, insured vault subscription for original wills, deeds, titles, seed-phrase backups and heirlooms, with a scripted release protocol for heirs, sold through estate attorneys as the bank box disappears.
customer: Estate-planning and elder-law attorneys as the channel, and their clients aged 55 to 85 whose plan says 'the original is in the safe deposit box'. Secondary: coin, gold and crypto holders, and small landlords and business owners holding original deeds and titles.
problem: Chase said in August 2025 that it would phase out all remaining safe deposit boxes nationwide, after it stopped new rentals in 2021. Capital One, Santander and Citizens exited earlier, and the total number of boxes has reportedly fallen from about 40M to an estimated 25M to 32M. Contents are not FDIC-insured, and no federal law governs boxes. On a death the bank typically freezes access until paperwork clears. The box was the default chain of custody for the paper that proves who owns what, and nothing has replaced it.
solution: Rent standardized boxes or sealed envelopes inside licensed, bonded vault partners. Each item gets a photo and hash inventory, and contents are insured under a valuables policy. The core product is a designated-heir protocol: on a death certificate plus an attorney letter or executor's letters, the vault releases to the named person after video attestation and dual control. Add periodic proof-of-life check-ins, an index the attorney can see, and an original-will custody service tied to the attorney's office.
why_now: Chase's nationwide phase-out (announced August 2025) removed the largest holder of boxes. The Great Wealth Transfer is under way. Retail gold and crypto holdings create new 'irreplaceable original' items such as seed backups and coins that people do not want in a home closet.
revenue_model: $15 to $35 per month per box, or $199 to $399 per year. A $99 onboarding and inventory fee. A $250 heir-release fee. A white-label or referral share of $5 to $10 per client per month for law firms. Margin on the insurance premium.
non_obvious_insight: The box was never about valuables. It was legal chain of custody for original paper, and banks are quitting because vault space is expensive real estate, not because the need went away. The product is the death protocol that banks never offered, since banks freeze access and a vault plus an attorney workflow can release to the named heir within days. Attorneys are the distribution because they carry malpractice risk when originals are lost.
first_30_days: Check whether your state regulates safe-deposit companies, then sign a white-label deal with one existing bonded vault or secure records-storage operator in a single metro. Draft the release protocol and client agreement with two estate attorneys. Present to 5 estate-planning firms and one senior center with a free 'Where are your originals?' inventory worksheet as the lead magnet. Sell 30 founding-member boxes at a discounted annual rate and run the first two mock heir releases to prove the protocol.

title: Remote-Driven Tractors for the Door-to-Door Leg
one_liner: Teleoperated tractors, driven from desks by remote drivers, that shuttle trailers between autonomous-truck terminals and customers' docks within about 30 miles.
customer: Autonomous-truck operators that need a handoff solution, carriers with hub networks, shippers with private yards, and ports and rail ramps.
problem: Hub-to-hub autonomy leaves door-to-door legs with 'hundreds of dollars' of human transfer cost per handoff, yet most freight is door-to-door. Short-haul and drayage driver turnover is high.
solution: Start on private yards, where no on-road rules apply, with retrofit teleop kits, multi-carrier connectivity and automatic safe-stop on link loss. A remote driver handles moves back to back with no deadhead, and automation covers straight segments. Extend later to short, permitted public-road hops at low speed. Price per move below a local yard driver plus deadhead.
why_now: Aurora (about 200 driverless trucks, 30,000 planned), Einride and Gatik are scaling the hub model, and the handoff economics are unresolved. Remote driving has been operating commercially in Europe and Las Vegas, and multi-carrier bonding makes latency manageable. Public-road legality for teleoperated heavy trucks in the US is unclear and needs checking.
revenue_model: $/move pricing, a monthly retainer per terminal, and equipment lease on the retrofit kits.
non_obvious_insight: The industry frames the last leg as an automation problem, but it is a utilization problem. One remote driver can serve several times more moves than a local driver who deadheads between yards, so teleop can beat both a human and a full autonomy stack on price for the next several years.
first_30_days: Sign a private yard (a rail ramp or DC with 20+ yard moves a day), retrofit one tractor with a rented teleop kit, and run a week of shadow operations. Price the pilot at about 20% below the current yard-jockey cost.

title: Medicaid Hours Wallet for Gig Workers
one_liner: A phone-based monthly proof-of-work ledger that turns gig, cash and self-employment activity into state-accepted documentation and 30-day cure packets, paid for by the Medicaid plans and health centers that lose revenue when members drop.
customer: Medicaid managed care organizations with expansion-adult lines, and FQHC and community health center networks. Medicaid is 43-50% of health center revenue, and an MCO is paid capitation per member-month. End users are expansion adults aged 19-64 with irregular income. The MCO or health center pays per retained member; the enrollee pays nothing.
problem: CMS's interim final rule (June 3, 2026) requires states to implement 80 hours a month of work or activity, or $580 a month in income, by Jan 1, 2027. Compliance is checked at application and at renewal, and a noncompliance notice gives 30 calendar days to cure. CBO projects about 4.8M coverage losses from work requirements, largely from reporting complexity. About 9 in 10 affected patients are expected to qualify for an exemption or already comply, yet many will still lose coverage on documentation. Nebraska went live May 1, 2026 with self-attestation, but about 28,000 people there must document twice a year and the state plans to move to verification.
solution: An enrollee-side SMS and app tool. It ingests bank and payment-app statements, gig platform earnings exports (Uber, DoorDash, Cash App, Venmo), pay stub photos and logged volunteer or class hours. It computes whether each month clears $580 or 80 hours and generates the state-specific verification packet. It sends look-back-month reminders and prepares the 30-day cure response. It flags likely exemption candidates, such as medically frail members, from plan claims data. The plan or clinic dashboard shows at-risk members and cure success. The tool only assists and never determines compliance, which is what federal rules allow plans to do.
why_now: The interim final rule was published June 3, 2026, and the national start date is Jan 1, 2027. Nebraska's live rollout is the preview of what other states will face when verification replaces self-attestation. CMS is encouraging automation, but states are spending on caseworker portals, notices and screening tools, not on income documentation for gig workers.
revenue_model: $3-8 per at-risk member per month billed to the MCO, or a success fee of $50-150 per member retained through renewal. FQHC SaaS at $2-5k per month per site with an outcomes dashboard. Later, state contracts for a self-employed and gig documentation module.
non_obvious_insight: Vendors such as Salesforce are building state-facing portals for applicants and caseworkers. The parties with a P&L at stake, the MCOs and health centers, are not yet being sold a member-side tool. KFF's roundup of state outreach plans covers notices, websites and screening tools but does not describe how self-employed or irregular income will be documented (https://www.kff.org/medicaid/medicaid-work-requirements-federal-outreach-requirements-and-state-plans/). State wage-data matching misses 1099, cash and gig work by design. Georgetown's CCF warns that 'verification in this context means burdensome documentation requirements for enrollees' (https://ccf.georgetown.edu/2026/05/11/the-new-medicaid-work-reporting-requirements-are-here-dont-let-the-nebraska-soft-start-fool-you/). The retention math is lopsided: a plan or clinic can pay a few dollars a month per member to protect several hundred dollars of monthly revenue. Sources: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/06/03/2026-11094/medicaid-program-community-engagement-requirement-for-certain-individuals and https://www.pointcare.com/blog/how-to-prevent-medicaid-coverage-gaps-in-2026
first_30_days: Build the Nebraska flow first, since it is already live. Recruit 50 gig and self-employed Medicaid enrollees through one FQHC partner. Measure how many can produce a compliant $580 or 80-hour packet within 30 days. Take those results to two MCO member-engagement and quality leads for a paid pilot. Sign an LOI with one health center network before Jan 1, 2027.

title: Physically Verified Protocol Skills for Lab Agents
one_liner: A registry of agent-executable bench protocols where every version has actually been run on real instruments in independent labs, with signed control readouts, like CI badges backed by experiments.
customer: AI-native biotech startups, academic labs and core facilities running agent-directed workflows on liquid handlers (Opentrons OT-2/Flex, Hamilton, Tecan), plus cloud-lab operators. Buyers are lab managers and automation leads. Individual protocol authors are the supply side.
problem: Agent 'skills' registries are the new package supply chain (about 20% of the OpenClaw skill registry was reportedly malicious, and Okta paid about $200M for Permiso to sandbox skills). In biology a bad skill is not just a leaked token. It is a wasted week of bench time, a contaminated line, or a biosafety event. The last roughly 10% of manual steps in a 5,000-action workflow is tacit knowledge nobody writes down. Anthropic found that robotic automation fit ad hoc molecular-biology workflows poorly, and that expert review and bench work were the bottleneck rather than compute.
solution: Publish protocols as versioned skills: robot script, agent-readable instructions, parameter bounds, expected control values and hazard flags. A release counts as 'verified' only after it runs on at least 3 independent partner instruments and posts raw plate-reader or qPCR files with pass/fail on Z' and control CVs. Agents (or their human owners) can only pull skills above a reproducibility threshold. Static checks flag off-protocol reagent additions, unusual volumes or temperatures and dual-use red flags. Start with about 25 workhorse assays: Golden Gate/Gibson assembly, transformation, qPCR setup, viability, ELISA and Bradford.
why_now: The skills-as-supply-chain scare of 2026 and the Permiso acquisition prove buyers will pay to trust agent skills. Frontier labs and startups are now wiring agents to physical labs (Anthropic's wet lab, Medra, Lila, Transfyr's $25M seed to capture bench actions). Nobody sells verified physical execution, only software scanning.
revenue_model: Subscription per lab ($300-1,000/month for verified-skill access and update alerts); per-protocol certification fees paid by protocol authors and vendors ($1-3K per validation cycle); revenue share to partner validation labs; enterprise private registry for pharma automation groups.
non_obvious_insight: In software, tests are free, so registries compete on code. In biology the test is an experiment, so the moat is a network of physical validation sites and the accumulated failure data, not the code. Whoever owns the 'passes on real hardware' stamp owns trust in agentic bench work, and it also becomes the natural biosafety screen for skills.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 academic labs that already own OT-2s (they are common and often underused). Pick 10 protocols and run each 3 times per site. Publish the raw data and pass rates publicly as the marketing. Offer free verified skills to 30 labs via bioRxiv/Reddit/Slack communities, then charge $500/month for early access to new verified skills, alerts and private forks. Target 10 paying labs by month 3.

title: Agent-Buyable Assay Storefronts With QC-Gated Escrow
one_liner: Turn idle university cores and orphaned biotech labs into machine-buyable assay shops where payment releases automatically only if the raw instrument data passes pre-agreed control checks.
customer: Sellers are university core facilities, small CROs and shuttered-biotech labs with idle instruments. Buyers are protein-design, synbio and 'AI scientist' teams whose agents generate thousands of candidates. Revenue comes from a take rate on transactions.
problem: Design-build-test is now bounded by assays, not DNA (the Weizmann 2.5 billion antibody fragments cost only EUR 38,000 in DNA synthesis). Yet bench services are sold by 'request a quote' forms and PDF emails that agents cannot use, and buyers cannot judge whether a result is real. NIH turbulence (grant caps, K99 restrictions, staff protections stripped) and biotech layoffs (15,000+ cuts) leave cores and dead-company labs with idle capacity and no sales function. Agent commerce already shows the pattern: RentAHuman had about 590,000 sign-ups against about 11,300 bounties, so supply is abundant and trusted demand is scarce.
solution: Each standardized assay (BLI/SPR binding, thermal shift, expression titer, mycoplasma test, mass-spec ID, sequencing verification) becomes an MCP or ACP offer with price, turnaround, sample requirements, shipping label and acceptance criteria. Money sits in escrow and releases when deterministic rules on the raw output pass (positive/negative control window, Z' above a threshold, expected ladder). A failure triggers an automatic rerun or refund, so no one argues about disputes.
why_now: Machine-payment rails shipped in 2026 (Stripe/Tempo MPP on March 18, x402 to the Linux Foundation in April, ACP/AP2). Frontier labs are running hundreds of parallel bio-agents. NIH funding instability is pushing cores to seek outside revenue, and biotech distress in 2026 is creating idle labs.
revenue_model: 5-10% take rate on assay orders, float and expedite fees on escrow, listing setup fees for sellers ($500-2,000), and a managed-account tier for large protein-design teams.
non_obvious_insight: The unsolved dispute problem in agentic commerce becomes tractable for physical science because instruments emit machine-checkable controls. Acceptance tests on raw files stand in for human judgment, and academic core capacity is the cheapest, most trustworthy supply pool exactly when NIH money is shaky.
first_30_days: Sign 5 cores (mass spec, BLI, sequencing, flow) and list 10 SKUs with fixed prices. Run everything semi-manually behind a simple API and Stripe. Offer $2K free-assay bounties to 10 protein-design groups (BindCraft/RFdiffusion users) and have their scripts place orders. Publish pass rates and turnaround. Charge 8% from day one.

title: Provenance Stamps for AI-Drafted Official Products
one_liner: A document layer that makes AI-assisted analytic and official products visibly claim-by-claim traceable, and refuses to export as official until unsupported claims are resolved.
customer: State and regional fusion centers, police intelligence units, commercial OSINT and threat-intel shops selling to government, and city attorneys' offices. DoD follows later via integrators.
problem: A SOCOM analyst's chatbot invented a ship's cargo manifest, and it was formatted into an official-looking intelligence summary before aircraft were airborne. Insiders say better models will fix hallucination. The real failure is laundered credibility: AI-formatted output looks signed and trusted.
solution: A Word and Docs add-in that tags every sentence as source-linked, analyst-asserted or model-generated. Model-generated claims carry a visible marker. Official templates and PDF export are blocked until each claim has a source or a named human sign-off. It produces a hashed provenance record for later review.
why_now: GenAI.mil hit more than 2M users in one week, and 100k custom agents exist. The SOCOM story is public, and government AI-governance guidance is hardening. Buyers can now cite a concrete incident.
revenue_model: $40-90 per user per month, with agency site licenses of $50-250K. Enterprise add-ons for audit reporting.
non_obvious_insight: The fix is friction, not accuracy. Sell a product that deliberately makes AI-drafted content look unofficial until a human has vouched for it, so trust cannot be laundered through formatting.
first_30_days: Ship the add-in for one document type, such as a threat bulletin. Recruit 3 fusion centers and 2 OSINT vendors as design partners. Build a demo that replays the SOCOM failure and shows it being blocked.

title: Overnight First-Call Co-op for Independent Funeral Homes
one_liner: A shared night-and-weekend answering, dispatch and chain-of-custody service so small funeral homes never lose a call at 2 a.m.
customer: Independent funeral homes, especially 1-3 director shops. NFDA counts 15,401 US funeral homes, about 75% family or privately owned. Hospice and hospital partners are the second audience.
problem: Small homes burn out staff on overnight first calls or miss them. Each service is worth several thousand dollars: SCI reports average revenue per service of $5,985. Hospitals want fast pickups, and chain-of-custody mistakes are catastrophic in an industry facing scrutiny after high-profile scandals.
solution: A shared first-call desk with trained answering, dispatch to a vetted licensed removal network, and a QR-tag custody app (ID verification, photos, timestamps) from bedside to the home's cooler. Add a hospital-facing release portal and overflow transfers later.
why_now: Consolidators keep gaining scale while independents face labor constraints. Volume is flat (SCI -1.4% in Q2 2026), so each lost call matters. Post-scandal regulatory attention raises the value of documented custody.
revenue_model: Per-dispatch fees ($175-$400 by distance), $199-$499/month retainers, and software add-ons.
non_obvious_insight: Independents fear losing the call more than losing on price, and the call is decided in the first hour. Owning that hour makes you the switching layer between hospitals and independents.
first_30_days: Pick one metro. Recruit 10 independents and 3 removal contractors. Run the phone desk yourself and charge about $250 per call. Log every call to build a service-level report.

title: Clinician-Prescribed AI Social Practice for Kids
one_liner: A bounded, transcript-visible role-play partner that speech-language pathologists prescribe to autistic and socially anxious kids, sold to districts that are legally obliged to deliver therapy minutes.
customer: School-district special-education departments, contract therapy staffing firms (SLP, psychology) and private pediatric therapy clinics.
problem: Insiders think kids plus AI is a no-go zone. Character.AI barred under-18s from open-ended chat in November 2025, and the FTC 6(b) inquiry and state laws (CA SB 243) followed. But districts must deliver IEP speech and social-communication minutes, SLP caseloads are huge and vacancies persist. Kids need many low-stakes repetitions between weekly 30-minute sessions.
solution: An anti-companion design: the SLP assigns scripted scenarios (ordering lunch, joining a game, handling teasing). There is no persona, no persistent memory and no free topics. Practice is recorded and the SLP dashboard produces the progress-monitoring data IEPs require. Parents can read transcripts. Voice-first, tuned for child speech, with no audio retention by default.
why_now: Regulators and lawsuits (Raine v. OpenAI, Pennsylvania v. Character.AI) closed the open-ended companion door, which makes scoped, clinician-in-the-loop tools the defensible lane. Speech models handle child speech far better than they did two years ago. Special-ed budgets are stretched (from memory).
revenue_model: Per-student annual licence ($150-400), much cheaper than added SLP hours at $60-100 an hour. Clinics pay per clinician seat.
non_obvious_insight: The regulated lane isn't closed, it just has a different buyer: a clinician with a legal duty to document. Designing it as the opposite of a companion (no persona, no memory, no free chat) makes it compliant by construction and defensible in the next lawsuit.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 practicing SLPs to script 30 scenarios. Build a voice prototype. Run a 4-week paid pilot with about 10 kids in one private clinic ($99 a month per child). Then approach one contract-therapy staffing firm with the pilot's progress-monitoring data.

title: Risk and Insurance Stack for Pickleball Venues
one_liner: Incident logging, e-waivers, court-safety audits and an insurance program that make independent racquet venues insurable at fair prices.
customer: Independent indoor and outdoor pickleball and padel venue operators, plus HOAs and municipal recreation departments.
problem: Indoor pickleball operators report difficulty finding coverage, typical policies carry $1-5M general liability, injuries rose about 6.8x between 2017 and 2022, and noise disputes now end in lawsuits. Insurers lack venue-level data, so they price the category rather than the operator.
solution: Step one: $149-299 per month software with e-waivers, incident reporting, a photo-evidence court, lighting and fencing audit checklist and staff training. Step two: use the aggregated data to place operators with specialty carriers as a broker or MGA and negotiate premium credits for documented venues.
why_now: Venue counts have boomed while commentators now say the boom is starting to crack, which makes insurers and lenders demand evidence; no standard exists.
revenue_model: SaaS $149-299 per venue per month plus 10-15 percent broker or MGA commission on premiums of $8-30k per policy.
non_obvious_insight: Data is the product: when insurers lack venue-level evidence they price to the average, so the operator who documents beats the average. Start as software, then capture the insurance economics.
first_30_days: Partner with a licensed broker, audit 10 venues in one metro, produce an insurer-ready risk dossier for each, and take 20 dossiers to two specialty carriers.

title: Staffed Junk Playgrounds as Apartment Amenity
one_liner: Adventure playgrounds with loose parts, dirt, tools and trained playworkers, installed on unused lots at family-heavy apartment communities and sold to landlords as a renewal lever.
customer: Owners and operators of garden-style, suburban and build-to-rent multifamily communities (200+ units, many households with children ages 5-12). Parents are the secondary payers via optional drop-in fees.
problem: Roughly 40 states now require schools to restrict phones, yet the 3-6pm window at home is where screen time actually happens. Australia's under-16 social media ban has reportedly changed daily use only slightly (about 58% still use daily vs about 60% before), a sign that removing a device without providing somewhere to go does little. Parents want unsupervised, physical, unstructured play but fear liability and have no safe place. Meanwhile landlords spend amenity budgets on gyms and coworking rooms nobody uses and lose family tenants to turnover that costs thousands of dollars per unit.
solution: A turnkey adventure playground service in the UK 'playwork' tradition: pallets, tires, rope, cardboard, sand, water, hammers and a supervised fire pit on an old parking lot or lawn, run 15-20 hours a week (after school and weekends) by trained playworkers who intervene as little as possible. The operator supplies the loose-parts kit, a written risk-benefit assessment, staff training, a background-check protocol and a specialty liability policy. The property signs a monthly contract, and families pay nothing or a small add-on. Tracked outcomes include tenant survey scores and renewal rates for families with school-age children.
why_now: Phone-free school laws spread across about 40 states by mid-2026 and the 'anxious generation' framing turned play-based childhood into a mainstream parenting goal. Free-range parenting statutes in a growing number of states reduce neglect-law fear. Build-to-rent operators are competing on amenities and retention. Nonprofit adventure playgrounds exist but cannot scale because of staffing and liability, which a landlord-funded model solves.
revenue_model: Service contract of about $3-5k per property per month (staff, materials, insurance, management), optional $15-20 per child drop-in for non-residents, and multi-property master agreements with regional operators. Ten properties gives roughly $400-600k in annual recurring revenue.
non_obvious_insight: The real buyer of 'screen-free childhood' is the landlord, not the parent. One prevented move-out saves thousands of dollars in turnover, so a single retained family pays for a month of the program, and kids' friendships create lock-in that no gym can. The barrier to adventure playgrounds was never demand, it was insurance and staffing, and packaging them as a managed property service turns a nonprofit hobby into infrastructure.
first_30_days: Find one friendly 300-unit community and offer an 8-week free trial in exchange for data. Spend about $2k on pallets, tires, rope and tools, hire two playwork or early-childhood students, and get a liability quote from a specialty broker. Survey tenants with kids before and after, and track leasing-team feedback. Photograph everything and pitch 20 regional property managers through local apartment associations and LinkedIn. Aim to convert the trial and one more property to paid contracts within 4-5 months.

title: Deadline-Proof AI Overflow and PII Shield for CPA Firms
one_liner: A browser extension that strips client SSNs, EINs and bank numbers before any AI tool sees them, and routes work to a compliant pay-as-you-go model when the firm's licensed AI hits its usage cap in the middle of a deadline.
customer: Accounting, tax and bookkeeping firms with 3 to 30 people, plus the MSPs that run their IT. All of them have written-security-program duties under the FTC Safeguards Rule.
problem: In 2026 vendors are moving to usage-based AI billing (Microsoft now uses Copilot Credits with administrator spending limits). When a firm's tool hits its cap mid-deadline, staff face three options: work stops, costs climb, or they improvise with personal consumer accounts. Uploading client statements and spreadsheets to unvetted tools breaks the Safeguards Rule's service-provider oversight requirement. Firms have no visibility into what left the building.
solution: A lightweight extension and gateway. First, it detects client PII (SSNs, EINs, account and routing numbers, dates of birth) in prompts and uploads and swaps in reversible tokens, with the mapping kept locally on the user's device. Second, it meters each seat's usage against the firm's licensed tools and, at 80% of a cap, offers an approved overflow route to a zero-retention model API billed at wholesale token cost plus a margin. Third, it writes an audit log that maps directly onto the firm's written information security program: who used what, which data classes were blocked, and which vendors were approved. Pre-purchased burst capacity is sold before each crunch (Oct 15 extension deadline, Mar 15, Apr 15).
why_now: The relevant CPA Practice Advisor article is dated Sept 28, 2026 (today). The Oct 15 extension deadline is 17 days away. Usage-based AI billing became normal this year. Firms are cutting headcount but software costs don't fall with it, so overflow spend competes with shrinking budgets.
revenue_model: $19 per seat per month for the shield and audit log, plus metered overflow at token cost +30%. Burst-capacity packs of $99 to $499 per season. MSPs and state CPA society partnerships get a channel margin of about 20%.
non_obvious_insight: The risk is not the AI model, it is the capacity cliff at the worst possible moment, which pushes careful staff into shadow tools. CPA Practice Advisor states: 'When a firm's AI tool hits its usage cap mid-deadline, staff often turn to free consumer tools', cites the FTC Safeguards Rule requirement for a written information security program and oversight of service providers, and quotes IBM's finding that high shadow-AI usage adds about $670,000 to breach costs, with 63% of breached organizations having no AI governance policy (https://www.cpapracticeadvisor.com/2026/09/28/token-limits-are-creating-a-shadow-ai-problem-for-accounting-firms/190633/). A companion piece shows why buying more seats isn't the answer: software costs stay flat when headcount falls, with contracts fixed until the notice deadline (https://www.cpapracticeadvisor.com/2026/09/03/why-client-software-costs-dont-fall-when-headcount-does-and-what-advisors-should-review/189557/).
first_30_days: Week 1: build the redaction extension for Chrome/Edge with regex plus a small detector, and a simple metering dashboard. Pitch it in accounting communities and state CPA society newsletters as a 'get through Oct 15' tool. Weeks 2 to 3: onboard 10 firms free for the extension season in exchange for testimonials and audit-log feedback. Week 4: convert to $19 per seat and sell burst packs ahead of the next crunch; approach two MSPs that serve CPA firms. Target: 8 paying firms and 1 MSP partner.

title: Loss Draft Desk for Storm Contractors
one_liner: Software and concierge service that gets contractors and homeowners through the mortgage servicer's loss-draft process, then advances cash against approved draws.
customer: Storm-restoration general contractors, roofers and owner-builders working on mortgage-encumbered repairs and rebuilds, starting with the Palisades and Eaton rebuild wave and Gulf Coast stragglers. Later, homeowners and the servicers' own vendor teams.
problem: The carrier pays, but the money is not free: the check names the mortgagee, and the servicer's loss-draft department decides whether to release it in one lump sum or in staged draws tied to inspections. Each servicer has its own packet (contractor W-9, license, signed contract, lien waivers, before/after photos, inspection scheduling) and its own cadence. Contractors carry 60-120 days of working capital risk, homeowners cannot start work, and adjusters take the blame for a delay that comes after the estimate is done.
solution: A draw-management platform: it reads the carrier's payment letter and the servicer's requirements, auto-builds and submits the servicer-specific packet, schedules and preps for inspections (checklist plus timestamped photo capture), chases the servicer, and shows the contractor and homeowner a live 'money timeline.' Phase two adds a draw advance: after the servicer approves a draw schedule, the platform advances 80-90% of the next draw in days, underwritten on proprietary servicer-by-servicer release data.
why_now: Florida's AOB ban (for policies since 2023) means contractors cannot be paid directly by carriers, so they must wait on homeowners and servicers. The LA fire rebuild in 2026-27 involves thousands of large, mortgage-encumbered claims and long draw schedules. Materials costs remain volatile, which squeezes contractor cash. Regulatory rules and GSE guidelines push servicers to release funds promptly after approving a repair plan but leave the mechanics unstandardized, creating a compliance-flavored process that software can systematize.
revenue_model: Flat $295-$495 per job, or 0.5-1% of funds released. Draw advances at 2-3% of advance amount plus a 30-60 day fee, funded by a warehouse credit line. Later, per-file fees from servicers who want clean packets and fewer complaint escalations.
non_obvious_insight: The real payment terms in disaster repair are the servicer's draw curve, not the insurance company's payment speed, and nobody publishes it. Whoever logs, servicer by servicer, days-to-first-draw, inspection pass rates and packet rejection reasons owns the underwriting data for the only safe lending against insurance proceeds.
first_30_days: Sign up 5 mid-size LA fire rebuild contractors and 5 Gulf Coast roofers and offer to run their next 3 jobs through the loss-draft process as a done-for-you service at $295 per job. Log every servicer requirement in a shared spreadsheet, then turn it into a rules engine. Interview 3 former loss-draft department employees for packet-rejection patterns. Start collecting draw-timeline data, which becomes the moat and the basis for a later advance product.

title: Actual-Play Sessions Turned Into Animated Episodes
one_liner: A pipeline that turns a tabletop RPG stream's audio and character art into a condensed animated episode using the cast's own voices, with human review.
customer: Actual-play shows and TTRPG creators with 3k-50k Patreon patrons, and TTRPG publishers wanting marketing series.
problem: Fans want animated adaptations, but animation costs millions. Creators have hundreds of hours of audio and no way to give patrons a visual product.
solution: Ingest the session audio and each creator's character art bible. An LLM editor condenses a 4-hour session into a 12-20 minute script. Video generation uses per-character references trained only on the creator's own art, with consenting voices and lip-sync, and a producer reviews each cut. Output includes premium-tier episodes and short clips for growth.
why_now: Video models now generate consistent characters with synced audio, and creators can use their own art and voices with disclosure, which sidesteps most of the AI-slop backlash.
revenue_model: $1.5-5k per episode or 20-30% of new patron revenue for 12 months, plus a licensing fee for publishers.
non_obvious_insight: The output is not cinema but the recap format, the 'previously on' fans share, and the same pipeline produces shorts that grow the channel. Consent and disclosure are the differentiators.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 mid-size actual-play creators. Produce one 90-second pilot for each from public sessions, and refine. Sell 3 paid episodes at $1.5k.

title: Virtual Detention Basin from Smart Cisterns
one_liner: Thousands of backyard tanks that pre-drain before forecast storms, coordinated like a virtual power plant for stormwater.
customer: Stormwater utilities and sewer districts under combined-sewer consent decrees, and cities running basement-flooding programs.
problem: Utilities spend billions on tunnels and tanks to control overflows and basement flooding, while private-lot storage sits unmanaged because each barrel is dumb. FEMA money is unstable, so cities want cheaper capacity.
solution: Forecast-controlled cisterns and rain gardens with low-cost cellular valves that pre-drain ahead of storms and hold water at the peak, driven by AI weather ensemble forecasts. The utility pays per managed gallon at peak. First product is a 200-tank pilot in one sewershed, retrofitting existing barrels with a roughly $150 controller.
why_now: AI weather ensembles (operational since 2025) make per-storm control affordable, cellular valves are cheap, and consent-decree deadlines and unstable FEMA funding push cities toward distributed capacity.
revenue_model: Per managed gallon or per tank-year utility contracts, plus grants and rebates covering hardware.
non_obvious_insight: A city's cheapest new detention basin is 10,000 backyards coordinated like a virtual power plant.
first_30_days: Identify 3 combined-sewer cities with rebate programs, retrofit 50 existing barrels with controllers, and measure peak outflow reduction.
